newsitem.title: USA: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD - Dow due for a breather.
newsitem.headline: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD - Dow due for a breather.

text.p: Two weeks and 300 Dow points into its election celebration, Wall Street is expected to pause for a much-needed rest this week after a string of eight straight record closing highs.

The surge, which began on Election Day and whose fury has at times has left market watchers puzzled, is finally showing some signs of wear, said analysts, several of whom are openly yearning for a respite.
"This market has a long way to go on the upside in the long-term," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments. "But for the near-term, we're in a danger zone."

The Dow industrials closed at 6348.03 on Friday, posting a 128.95 point rise for the week. In the last two weeks, which includes a 19.8 point gain in the session before Election Day, the Dow is up a whopping 326.13 points, or 5.4 percent.
Over each of the last eight of those sessions, the Dow has closed at a new record high, a streak that has sent Wall Street historians scurrying to find the last time blue chips managed such a run.
In the process, the rally left skeptics burned again, although few were shaking off their skepticism.

"The trend-followers are in command of this market for the time being and those of us who have been fighting the tape have been wrong," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer and Co.
Despite the stubborn nature of the run-up, which has resisted repeated predictions of a pause, analysts remain convinced some backtracking is inevitable.
"Wall Street tends to go to extremes, and over the last couple of days we have gotten a little ahead of ourselves," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.
However, as Bleier noted, the strongest buying interest remained largely focused on top-name blue chip stocks, a symptom of investors' lock-step approach to the market.
"The market is in its most classic herd mentality," he said. "All of the institutions are chasing the same 'nifty-fifty' style names."

Most visible among those buyers remain mutual fund managers, such as at Fidelity's flagship Magellan Fund, which reported last week that it boosted equities by five percent to 88.9 percent of overall assets as of the end of September.
For fund managers, who have enough work finding ways to allocate the new cash that continues to flow to accounts, finding a home for cash raised by selling positions only adds to the burden.
"The problem is if you sell something, you then have the problem of buying something else that is equally overpriced," Metz said.
The other problem is the investor-friendly economic environment of moderate growth without inflation, which makes justifying selling a tough task.
"With long bonds yielding less than 6.5 percent and cash at under five percent, there's really no alternative," said Edgar Peters, chief investment strategist at PanAgora Asset Management Inc.
"As long as interest rates stay low, the market can continue rising because there's no reason for people to sell stocks," he said.
Upcoming economic data are unlikely to change that, as the week's calendar does not include any Wall Street focal points.
Tuesday will bring weekly retail sales figures and October housing starts, which are expected to edge higher to an annualized 1.44 million units.
Other data include international trade balance figures, due Wednesday, and weekly jobless claims, due Thursday. Economists expect new claims to rise by 4,000 to 332,000.
-- Wall Street desk, 212-859-1730
